analysis.one_liner: Suspends oil companies' federal royalty waivers when prices are high and directs the royalties to disaster relief and home energy aid.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in House subcommittees until the 109th Congress ended, and all ten of its sponsors were Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: After Hurricane Katrina drove oil and gas prices sharply higher, this bill would have taken away a break that lets companies pump oil and gas from federal lands without paying royalties. The waiver would switch off automatically whenever average crude oil topped $40 a barrel or natural gas topped $5 per thousand cubic feet, and the money collected would go to disaster relief and to LIHEAP, the federal program that helps low-income households pay heating and cooling bills. The bill was referred to four House committees, then to three subcommittees, and no committee ever acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households who get help paying energy bills through LIHEAP, and communities recovering from disasters like Hurricane Katrina, who would share in the new royalty money. Taxpayers generally would gain because the public would collect royalties on federal oil and gas during high-price periods instead of the money going to producers.

how_it_helps.text: When prices exceed set thresholds, companies producing oil and gas from federal lands would have to pay royalties they were otherwise excused from paying, with the revenue available for disaster relief and the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program.
The thresholds are automatic, based on Energy Information Administration price data, so relief flows to households exactly when energy prices are at their highest.

During the fall of 2005, crude oil prices were well above $40 per barrel, so the bill's provisions would have applied immediately and redirected royalty money toward Katrina recovery and heating assistance.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding leases on federal lands, including offshore submerged lands, which would pay royalties on their production whenever prices exceeded the bill's thresholds — in 2005, a period of historically high prices, that would have been most production.

drawbacks.text: Removing royalty relief when prices are highest could discourage production at exactly the moment supply is strained, which producers argued could nudge prices up rather than down.

The bill gives the President discretion over how to spend the collected royalties outside the normal congressional appropriations process, a design choice critics of broad executive spending discretion routinely oppose.
The price triggers are fixed numbers rather than tied to long-term averages, so a brief price spike could switch the waiver off even in periods when producers face genuinely high costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have shifted real money from energy producers to low-income energy assistance and disaster relief at the moment prices were punishing households hardest. The main cost is borne by a specific industry rather than spread across the public, and the risk that removing the waiver slightly discourages drilling is modest compared with the direct benefit of funding home energy aid during a price spike. Its main design weakness is executive discretion over the money, but that is a process question, not a reason the money is misplaced.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four committees and then three subcommittees, none of which ever held a hearing or vote on it, and it died when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the bill on September 8, 2005, less than two weeks after Hurricane Katrina struck the Gulf Coast.
The House referred it to the Natural Resources, Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, and Education and the Workforce Committees on the day it was introduced.

Over the following five weeks it was passed down to three subcommittees — economic development and emergency management, energy and mineral resources, and energy and air quality — and finally to the Education Reform Subcommittee in October 2005.
No committee or subcommittee ever reported the bill, and there is no record of any hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies holding federal leases kept receiving royalty relief through a period of record-high prices, and no new royalty money went to disaster relief or low-income energy aid. The bill's sponsors and the households it aimed to help got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Edward J. Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 8, 2005, and used his Natural Resources Committee seat to press the royalty-relief issue, though he held no scheduling power over the bill.

for.name: 9 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Committee and subcommittee chairs of the four referring committees
against.role: Natural Resources, Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, and Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in any of the four committees or three subcommittees it was assigned to, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Republican House majority
against.role: Held the committee chairs and floor schedule in the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Controlled which bills reached the floor; no version of the royalty-relief suspension was ever brought to a House vote.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; the bill died in committees chaired by Republicans without any recorded vote to measure party positions.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal lands (onshore and offshore leaseholders)
industries.note: The bill would have ended automatic royalty waivers — the industry's break from paying the government a share of production value — whenever prices exceeded $40 oil or $5 gas. In 2005's record-price market, that meant billions in royalties would have shifted from producers to disaster relief and low-income energy aid, so the industry's interest in the bill's failure ran directly against the households the bill targeted.
